titles.183: Annotatio II §.V open: Dissensus on Coena words/presence grows via Ubiquity controversy — Luther in dispute heat (Greater Confession)
titles.184: Annotatio II §.V: Ubiquity drawn to ease corporeal Coena defense — afterward neglected
titles.185: Annotatio II §.V: Brentius & Jacob Andreae resume ubiquity — Heshusius contradicts though sharing Coena view
titles.186: Annotatio II §.V: Marbach Senior confirms with harsher theses — human nature called God; Fechtius reports

latin.183:
§. V.
Quô ipsô Dissensus Protestantium, in interpretatione Verborum Coenae & in Praesentiae Corporis Christi modo, in usu Sacrae Coenae, exorsus, Incrementa cepit, per Controversiam de Ubiquitate Corporis Christi, à Luthero quidem in aestu disputationis semel atque iterum, duobus potissimum Confessionis suae majoris locis, Calixto allegatis, loc. cit. num. 41. 42.
latin.184: eam in rem adductam, ut corporalem in Coena S. Corporis Christi praesentiam tantò faciliùs defendere valeret, sed posteà neglectam,
latin.185: à Brentio verò & Jacobo Andrea (uti annot. precedenti §. 14. diximus) contradicente tamen ejusdem licèt sententiae de Coena participe Tillemanno Heshusio (videatur Hospin. Hist. Sacr. pag. 40.) reassumtam
latin.186: & à Marbachio Sen. aliis etiam propositionibus similibus & absurdioribus confirmatam defensamque, quibus Humanam Christi Naturam vel DEum ipsum rectè dici posse, ausus est affirmare, id quod ipse Celeberr. Fechtius refert, in Supplem. Historiae Eccl. pag. 30. Conf. Hospin. Concord. discord. cap. 55.;
latin.187: à Torgensibus in priori Conventu, anno 1574. habito, Articulô 4. rejectam rursus,
latin.188: in posteriori, anni 1576. (in quo, Corpore Doctrinae Philippicô abrogatô, in ejus locum Novum hodieq; Formulâ Concordiae comprehensum Doctrinae Lutheranae Corpus successit) tacitam, tandemque à Patribus Bergensibus de Potentiali explicatam, in solid. Explicat. & Declarat. Artic. Controv. pag. mihi p. 754. Edit. in 4to. Anno 1580.

pass_a.183: §. V. By which very thing the Dissensus of the Protestants, having begun in the interpretation of the Words of the Supper and in the mode of the Presence of Christ's Body in the use of the Holy Supper, took Increments, through the Controversy concerning the Ubiquity of Christ's Body, brought to that purpose by Luther indeed once and again in the heat of disputation, chiefly in two places of his Greater Confession, alleged by Calixtus, in the place cited, numbers 41 and 42.
pass_a.184: it having been brought in for that purpose, so that he might be able to defend the corporeal presence of Christ's Body in the Holy Supper so much the more easily, but afterward neglected,
pass_a.185: but resumed by Brentius and Jacob Andreae (as we said in the preceding Annotation §. 14), Tillemann Heshusius nevertheless contradicting — although a sharer of the same opinion concerning the Supper (see Hospinian, Historia Sacramentaria, page 40) —
pass_a.186: and confirmed and defended by Marbach the Elder also by other similar and more absurd propositions, by which he dared to affirm that Christ's Human Nature can rightly be called even God Himself — which the most celebrated Fechtius himself reports in the Supplement to Ecclesiastical History, page 30; compare Hospinian, Concordia discordans, chapter 55;
pass_a.187: rejected again by the Torgau men in the earlier Convent held in the year 1574, in Article 4,
pass_a.188: silent in the later one of the year 1576 (in which, the Philippist Body of Doctrine having been abrogated, there succeeded in its place the New Body of Lutheran Doctrine still today comprehended in the Formula of Concord), and at last explained by the Bergen Fathers concerning the Potential — in the Solid Declaration and Explanation of the Controverted Articles, page (mine) 754, edition in quarto, year 1580.

183: §. V. That same Protestant split — begun over how the Supper words are read and over the mode of Christ's bodily presence in the Holy Supper's use — then grew through the controversy on the ubiquity of Christ's body.
Luther himself, once and again in the heat of debate, had drawn it in, chiefly from two places in his Greater Confession — the ones Calixtus cites at loc. cit. nos. 41–42.
184: He brought ubiquity in so he could defend a corporeal presence of Christ's body in the Holy Supper more easily — then later let it drop.
185: Brentius and Jacob Andreae took it up again (as we noted in the preceding Annotation, §.14) — even though Tillemann Heshusius, who shared their Supper view, contradicted them (see Hospinian, Historia Sacramentaria, p. 40).
186: Marbach the Elder then confirmed and defended it with further like — and even more absurd — propositions, daring to say Christ's human nature can rightly be called God Himself.
So Fechtius reports in his Supplement to Ecclesiastical History, p. 30 (cf. Hospinian, Concordia discordans, ch. 55).
187: The Torgau assembly of 1574 rejected it again in Article 4.
188: In the later Torgau meeting of 1576 it went silent — the year the Philippist Corpus Doctrinae was set aside and today's Formula of Concord body of Lutheran doctrine took its place.
At last the Bergen Fathers explained it as potential, in the Solid Declaration and Explanation of the Controverted Articles (my copy p. 754; 4to ed. 1580).
